item.title: Cornell Bans Fraternity Parties and Adds Sexual Assault Investigators
item.description:
Cornell University has banned parties at fraternity houses for the rest of the academic year and will add experienced sexual assault investigators to work with its police force in response to a student’s allegations of gang rape in October 2024.

The university announced the changes on Tuesday as it tried to reassure students, faculty and alumni that it is addressing the ongoing crisis set off several weeks ago by the lawsuit filed by a former undergraduate, known as Jane Doe.

“We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action,” Michael I. Kotlikoff, the president of Cornell, announced in a letter to the campus on Tuesday. “Cornell must be a place where safety is not an open question.”

The lawsuit shocked the campus and nation not only because of its allegations of rape, but also because it put on full display how fraternity members exchanged Snapchat messages using crude and dehumanizing language to describe the woman and what was taking place.

The announcement on Tuesday aims to also address the social culture at Cornell that set the stage for the alleged assault, Dr. Kotlikoff said.

“I am deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024, and appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community,” he said.

The most immediate change is a ban on all parties and social events in fraternity houses at Cornell for the remainder of the academic year, a sweeping measure on a campus where one-third of students are part of Greek life. Dr. Kotlikoff, in an interview on Tuesday, noted that since the pandemic, fraternity parties had been pushed even more to the center of student life.

“There is an issue, post-Covid, of what are the options for students in a town like Ithaca,” he said. “Many, many bars and venues went out of business and did not come back.”

The moratorium, which comes days before Homecoming weekend, will allow for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether it can safely resume, Dr. Koltikoff said.

“This is a step that we need to take at this point in time to force a reset,” said Anne Smalling, the chair of Cornell’s board of trustees, in an interview. “It’s incumbent on us to try and find other ways for these kids to engage in social settings.”

The campus will also enhance support for survivors of sexual assault, including by adding staffing to its civil rights office to help those who report incidents navigate what has been described as a complicated bureaucratic system. The university said that it would also work with the New York State Police to allow their “experienced, trauma-informed criminal investigators, who are independent of Cornell University” to investigate allegations of sexual assault, and to prepare “comprehensive investigative summaries for the appropriate law enforcement agency.”

Those changes seek to address some of the gaps in Cornell’s response that were highlighted by Jane Doe’s experience. Though she was interviewed at length by Cornell police in November 2024, the woman’s statement was condensed to a six-page summary for the district attorney that omitted a direct allegation from her stating that she was “100 percent certain” she had been raped.

The district attorney, Matthew Van Houten, decided not to prosecute. He also declined an offer from the Cornell University Police Department to review additional evidence, files obtained by The New York Times showed. In late September, after Jane Doe filed her lawsuit, he reopened a criminal investigation, which has since been taken over by Letitia James, the New York attorney general, at the request of Gov. Kathy Hochul.

None of the accused men have been charged with a crime, and all have denied wrongdoing.

On a deeper level, the reforms will try to address the social context of drug and alcohol abuse and attitudes toward women surfaced by Jane Doe’s allegations, Dr. Kotlikoff said in the letter.

Jane Doe, and several men whom she accused of assaulting her, drank alcohol and ingested ketamine at the fraternity house, the lawsuit said. She alleged that no one intervened to help her through the long night during which she said she was assaulted.

Cornell will enhance existing education and programming “to address the bystander effect and the duty of care we owe each other,” Dr. Kotlikoff announced. The university will also accelerate the implementation of other changes recommended by a 2025 task force on campus sexual assault, including a public health campaign about sexual violence and “expanded training for students, leaders and residential staff.”

Whether the changes will go far enough to address the anger on campus sparked by Jane Doe’s allegations remains an open question. Students have held protests, and the university’s faculty senate gave notice of a rare resolution of no confidence in the administration over the handling of the allegations.

Missing from the letter were any announcements of firings or personnel changes among Cornell administrators, or an explanation of why these steps were only being taken now, when university administrators have known about the gang rape allegations since 2024.

The letter also didn’t announce a pause on fraternity and sorority rushing for new students, as some on campus have demanded.

Despite the district attorney’s decision to not prosecute the case in 2024, Cornell’s Title IX office conducted a lengthy investigation in early 2025, in which it interviewed six of the seven alleged assailants and dozens of witnesses.

In the days after the alleged assault, some of the men coordinated to try to contain rumors about what had happened and sought to reassure Jane Doe that the gossip would blow over, text messages between the men revealed in the investigation showed.

After 12 days of hearings in March 2025, a panel of Cornell staff and faculty found sufficient evidence of sexual assault to expel two of the men and suspend two others. The three remaining men received lighter punishments, including having to study sexual harassment, social media use and bystander intervention, and write “reflection papers,” the documents obtained by The Times showed.

The fraternity, Chi Phi, was barred from campus, and its stately Tudor mansion remains closed.

Thomas Giuffra, an attorney for Jane Doe, praised the changes as moves in the right direction. While they come too late to protect Ms. Doe, he said, “these steps will hopefully go a long way to help ensure that there are no more Jane Does.”

Campus was quiet on Tuesday, the last day of fall break. But some students who were interviewed said that while they supported many of the changes, the ban on parties did not make sense.

“Banning parties now doesn’t do anything to fix what has happened,” said Ryan Nazari, a Cornell freshman. He wanted additional consequences to focus more squarely on the accused men and university officials, rather than all campus fraternities.

“It is more of a punishment on the entire student body,” Mr. Nazari said.

Finn Clancy, a senior majoring in biology and society, thought the ban could prove counterproductive.

“It’s slightly naïve of Cornell,” he said, “to think that these parties won’t happen.” He said younger students might flock to Collegetown, the Ithaca neighborhood where he lives, for off-campus parties that are outside of the university’s purview.

Hurubie Meko, Zane Irwin and Mack Liederman contributed reporting.

item.title: ‘I’m Personally Sorry’: Cornell’s President Acknowledges Missteps
item.description:
The president of Cornell University said on Tuesday that he learned that a student had reported being gang-raped at a fraternity party on campus shortly after she first came forward in November 2024.

But in the months that followed, he said, he did not follow up with her or seek to learn whether any of the accused men had been punished.

The president, Michael Kotlikoff, did not know that the woman had dropped out of Cornell until she filed a lawsuit last month under the pseudonym Jane Doe, he said in an interview with The New York Times.

“The fact that Jane Doe experienced what she experienced at Cornell is something that I am personally sorry for,” Dr. Kotlikoff said. “And I think this entire campus is sorry that occurred.”

During the 90-minute interview — the first Dr. Kotlikoff has given since the lawsuit was filed — he expressed anguish and horror over the events that have plunged his administration into crisis, and seemed to be pleading for time to confront the scandal. He also indicated he would not resign, even as he acknowledged that confidence in his leadership had been shaken.

“I’ve heard enough from the community that there is a loss of trust,” he said, later adding: “People are angry. I understand that anger.”

The lawsuit accused seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity of pressuring Jane Doe to take ketamine before sexually assaulting her at a party in their fraternity house October 2024. All the men named in the lawsuit have denied wrongdoing, and none have been charged with a crime.

Its filing on Sept. 16 touched off a fierce debate about consent and sexual assault on college campuses and led to intense scrutiny of Dr. Kotlikoff and Cornell. The school’s faculty senate is expected to hold a rare vote of no confidence in the president later this month.

Even as he acknowledged anger over his handling of the rape allegation, Dr. Kotlikoff, 75, at other times spoke with an almost clinical detachment about the alleged assault and the school’s response. He repeatedly referred to his creation of a presidential task force in February 2025 to address sexual assault on campus as a sign of his administration’s seriousness.

“We don’t set up a presidential task force for minor issues,” he said, adding that the panel introduced orientation training on sexual assault and “bystander responsibilities” for all new students earlier this year.

He was joined during Tuesday’s interview by Anne Smalling, chair of Cornell’s board of trustees, in an implicit endorsement of his continued leadership of the 26,000-student campus. Members of the 64-member board, however, have been largely silent on the question of the president’s future.

The school appeared to be still scrambling to contain the crisis on Tuesday. Shortly after the interview, Dr. Kotlikoff announced that Cornell would ban parties at fraternity houses for the rest of the academic year and add experienced sexual assault investigators to work with its campus police force.

Hours later, Cornell admissions officials sent an email to high school counselors acknowledging that they might feel conflicted about their students applying to the Ivy League school, and stressed that psychological and spiritual counseling is available to students they have sent there.

“We know that some of you may have mixed feelings about recommending Cornell to students now or in the future,” the email read.

In the interview, Dr. Kotlikoff said the steps taken by the school were meant to reassure parents who were considering sending their children to Cornell that they would be safe.

“I’ve had a number of conversations with parents,” he said. “I think this is a difficult conversation, particularly with the public that’s gotten so much different information about what actually went on and aren’t aware of these processes, and the complexity of a Title IX process,” which investigates potential violations of federal civil rights law on campuses.

He added that the administration wants parents and students to know that “we take the issue seriously, that we respond, that we heard the concerns, and we’re responding in specific ways that address those concerns.”

Dr. Kotlikoff said he and other school officials did not have a full picture of Jane Doe’s allegations and the subsequent investigation until earlier this month, when The Times published articles based on more than 1,000 pages of confidential records amassed during the university’s Title IX investigation in 2025. He said that, at the time, he was determined to allow that inquiry to be undertaken independently, and, to respect students’ privacy, did not ask about the results.

“I do think it’s important to understand we have more information now than we had at that time,” he said.

But experts in federal civil rights law said Dr. Kotlikoff most likely could have examined any of the material gathered during the investigation after the proceedings ended in the summer of 2025.

“Generally speaking, university presidents can be given access to completed Title IX investigative files when reviewing those materials serves a legitimate institutional purpose,” said Scott Schneider, a Title IX lawyer and adviser, adding that neither civil rights laws nor student privacy laws bar that access.

Dr. Kotlikoff also said he was not informed when the Tompkins County district attorney declined to bring charges in the case. And he said that, in hindsight, he felt he should have been alerted when Jane Doe withdrew from the school.

As a result of the investigation, two of the fraternity members were expelled and two were suspended. Another, who had already graduated, was barred from campus. The remaining men were handed lighter punishments.

The Title IX investigation also found heavy use of ketamine and alcohol by the Cornell students. Dr. Kotlikoff acknowledged that drugs and alcohol remain a problem at Cornell, which is in a relatively isolated community four hours north of New York City, but said other schools confront similar issues.

“I think that this is a problem that relates to 20-year-olds, 21-year-olds leaving home for the first time, coming into an environment where there’s access to alcohol, where there is unfortunately in some cases access to drugs. And they’re not prepared. And of course they’ve been exposed to social media, pornography, misogyny.

“This is a challenge for us, we have to respond by building character, judgment, responsibility, care for each other,” he said.

Dr. Kotlikoff and Ms. Smalling, the first woman to lead the board and a third-generation graduate of Cornell, said they hoped the university could become a role model in how to handle these issues. Both had children in the Greek system at Cornell.

“What Mike and his team are doing is facing the problem head on, taking action, listening to the community, understanding the issues, trying to find solutions, looking for ways to improve, looking for ways to be better,” Ms. Smalling said.

Last week, the university named Sally Yates, the former acting U.S. attorney general, to lead an independent internal review of the school’s handling of the case and issue recommendations for overhauling the system.

Neither Dr. Kotlikoff nor Ms. Smalling were willing to commit to a time frame for that investigation. Ms. Smalling said that despite the external pressures on university leadership, it was imperative that Ms. Yates be given a wide berth to conduct the most thorough investigation possible.

“A horrible event happened at Cornell University,” he said. “How do we make that into something where we now lead in this area and become known for having responded to it in the appropriate way? That, to me, is the challenge of my term.”

Hurubie Meko and Michael C. Bender contributed reporting.
